promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Phospholipids form a bilayer by themselves
The bilayer is a barrier
Osmosis and aquaporins
Pump proteins: active transport
The fluid mosaic model
Fatty acids and fluidity (HL)
Vesicles form and fuse because membranes are fluid (HL)
Gated ion channels in neurons (HL)
The sodium–potassium pump (HL)
Glucose cotransport: indirect active transport (HL)
What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
Why keep the nucleus and cytoplasm apart
How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
Why the nucleus has a double membrane with pores (HL)
Vesicles and clathrin (HL)

questions.q: A lipid is found to form a continuous sheet-like bilayer when shaken with water. Which property must the lipid have?
options: It must be entirely hydrophobic, so that all of its molecules cluster together away from water.
It must be amphipathic, with a hydrophilic region and a hydrophobic region in each molecule.
It must be able to form covalent bonds with neighbouring lipid molecules in the sheet.
It must be acted on by an enzyme that assembles the molecules into the bilayer.
optionWhy: A student who thinks lipids are simply water-repelling picks this. In fact an entirely hydrophobic lipid would separate as a droplet; a sheet needs a hydrophilic part that stays in contact with water.
Only amphipathic lipids form bilayers: the hydrophilic regions face the water on each side and the hydrophobic regions form the core. Phospholipids are the main example in cell membranes.
A student who expects the sheet to be a covalent polymer picks this. In fact a bilayer is held together only by hydrophobic interactions and other weak forces.
A student who thinks bilayers must be built picks this. In fact the bilayer forms spontaneously; the test in the stem involves only lipid and water, with no enzyme.
questions.explain: Only amphipathic lipids form bilayers: the hydrophilic regions face the water on each side and the hydrophobic regions form the core. Phospholipids are the main example in cell membranes.

questions.q: Which of these particles crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer, with no proteins present, least readily?
options: A carbon dioxide molecule, which is larger than a water molecule
An oxygen molecule, which needs a protein to cross the bilayer
A sodium ion, which is small but charged and hydrophilic
A water molecule, which is very small and also polar
optionWhy: A student who ranks particles by size alone picks this. In fact carbon dioxide is non-polar, so it passes readily between the hydrophobic tails despite its size.
A student who thinks nothing crosses the bilayer without a protein picks this. In fact oxygen is small and non-polar and crosses by simple diffusion between the phospholipids.

The hydrophobic core has very low permeability to hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules. A charged sodium ion cannot enter the hydrocarbon core, so it has the lowest permeability of the four.

A student who thinks water cannot cross a bilayer at all without aquaporins picks this. In fact water is small enough to pass slowly between the phospholipids; a charged ion is far less permeable than water.
questions.explain: The hydrophobic core has very low permeability to hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules. A charged sodium ion cannot enter the hydrocarbon core, so it has the lowest permeability of the four.

questions.q: An animal cell with a cytoplasmic solute concentration of 0.30 mol dm⁻³ is placed in a solution with a solute concentration of 0.10 mol dm⁻³. The membrane is impermeable to the solute. What happens?
options: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, because water moves from the higher to the lower solute concentration.
Net water movement is into the cell, because more free water molecules hit the membrane from the outside.
Solute diffuses out of the cell until both sides reach 0.20 mol dm⁻³, and water then follows the solute out.
No water crosses the membrane, because the cell membrane has no aquaporins to let water pass.
optionWhy: A student who applies 'high to low' to the solute picks this. In fact net water movement is from the lower solute concentration (0.10) to the higher (0.30), so water enters the cell.

The solution outside has the lower solute concentration and so a higher proportion of free water molecules. Water molecules move randomly in both directions, but more cross inwards than outwards, so the net movement is into the cell.
A student who treats osmosis as solute diffusion picks this. In fact the stem says the membrane is impermeable to the solute, so the solute cannot move; it is water that crosses.
A student who thinks aquaporins are the only route for water picks this. In fact water can cross the bilayer slowly without them, so osmosis still occurs; aquaporins only increase its rate.
questions.explain: The solution outside has the lower solute concentration and so a higher proportion of free water molecules. Water molecules move randomly in both directions, but more cross inwards than outwards, so the net movement is into the cell.

questions.q: Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?
options: Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.
Nitrate is taken up by facilitated diffusion through channels, which use ATP to move ions across against the gradient.
optionWhy: Uptake against a concentration gradient requires active transport, which uses energy from ATP. ATP is regenerated by cell respiration, so depriving the roots of oxygen reduces ATP supply and the pumps slow down.

A student who thinks active transport is just faster diffusion picks this. In fact nitrate is moving from a lower to a higher concentration, which diffusion cannot do in any direction; only pumps using ATP can.

A student who does not connect the ATP used by pumps to respiration picks this. In fact the cell's ATP is regenerated continuously by respiration and is used up within seconds if respiration stops, so removing oxygen from an aerobic cell soon halts active transport.
A student who thinks channels use ATP picks this. In fact facilitated diffusion is passive and cannot move ions against a gradient; that is the role of pumps.
questions.explain: Uptake against a concentration gradient requires active transport, which uses energy from ATP. ATP is regenerated by cell respiration, so depriving the roots of oxygen reduces ATP supply and the pumps slow down.

questions.q: Membrane proteins from a mouse cell and from a human cell were labelled with different coloured markers and the two cells were fused. After about 40 minutes the two colours were fully intermixed over the surface of the fused cell. What does this show?
options: Proteins can move laterally through the bilayer, so the membrane is fluid and proteins are not held in a fixed pattern.
The membrane developed gaps as it became more fluid, allowing the labelled proteins to leak through them.
The proteins from the two cells were covalently bonded into a single new continuous sheet during fusion.
The proteins remained in fixed positions but the mosaic pattern was rearranged by the fusion event.
optionWhy: If the proteins had been fixed in place, each colour would have stayed on its own half. Their mixing shows that proteins move sideways through the fluid phospholipid bilayer, which is what 'fluid' means in the fluid mosaic model.
A student who thinks 'fluid' means leaky picks this. In fact the bilayer stays continuous; proteins mixed by moving sideways within the plane of the membrane, not through gaps in it.
A student who expects membrane components to be covalently linked picks this. In fact no bonds form between the proteins; they mix because the bilayer is fluid and they can diffuse through it.
A student who thinks 'mosaic' means a fixed arrangement picks this. In fact the proteins moved: fusion joins the membranes but does not move a protein from one half to the other.
questions.explain: If the proteins had been fixed in place, each colour would have stayed on its own half. Their mixing shows that proteins move sideways through the fluid phospholipid bilayer, which is what 'fluid' means in the fluid mosaic model.

questions.q: In an investigation, fish of one species were kept at 5 °C or at 25 °C for several weeks. The membrane phospholipids of the fish kept at 5 °C contained a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids than those of the fish kept at 25 °C. What is the best explanation?
options: At 5 °C unsaturated fatty acids are needed to make the membranes more rigid, so that they hold their shape firmly in the cold.
At 5 °C the extra unsaturated fatty acids insulate the cells against heat loss, as fat does in polar animals.
At 5 °C membranes rich in saturated fatty acids would stiffen, so the fish increase unsaturated ones to stay fluid.
At 5 °C the fish's membranes are already more fluid because of the cold, so unsaturated fatty acids are added to make them stronger.
optionWhy: A student who has swapped the effects of the two types of fatty acid picks this. In fact unsaturated fatty acids lower the melting point and make membranes more fluid, not more rigid.
A student who thinks in terms of insulating fat picks this. In fact a membrane two molecules thick provides no insulation; the change in composition is about keeping the bilayer fluid.

Unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, so a higher proportion keeps the membrane fluid and flexible at the low temperature. Organisms living in cold habitats show the same pattern as an adaptation: cold-water fish have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes than related warm-water fish.
A student who reverses the effect of temperature on fluidity picks this. In fact cold makes a bilayer less fluid, not more, and it is saturated fatty acids that add strength.
questions.explain: Unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, so a higher proportion keeps the membrane fluid and flexible at the low temperature. Organisms living in cold habitats show the same pattern as an adaptation: cold-water fish have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes than related warm-water fish.

questions.q: At a synapse, neurotransmitter stored in vesicles is released into the synaptic cleft. How does the neurotransmitter leave the presynaptic neuron?
options: The vesicle bursts inside the neuron and the neurotransmitter diffuses out through the lipid bilayer.
The vesicle docks at a channel protein through which the neurotransmitter is passed out of the cell.
The vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane by exocytosis, releasing the contents outside.
The vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, a passive process since no pump protein is involved.
optionWhy: A student who pictures 'release' as bursting picks this. In fact the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and its contents are released outside without crossing a bilayer.
A student who expects all export to go through a protein picks this. In fact exocytosis involves fusion of two fluid membranes, not passage through a channel.

Neurotransmitter release is an example of exocytosis: the vesicle moves to the plasma membrane, the two fluid bilayers merge and the neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic cleft. The process requires ATP.
A student who thinks 'no pump' means 'passive' picks this. In fact exocytosis requires ATP to move the vesicle and bring about fusion, so it is an active process.
questions.explain: Neurotransmitter release is an example of exocytosis: the vesicle moves to the plasma membrane, the two fluid bilayers merge and the neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic cleft. The process requires ATP.

questions.q: Acetylcholine released at a synapse binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. What happens as a result?
options: The receptor opens and the acetylcholine molecules pass through it into the postsynaptic neuron.
The receptor uses ATP to pump sodium ions into the postsynaptic neuron, depolarizing it.
The receptor stays closed until the membrane potential changes, then it opens.
The receptor's channel opens and sodium ions diffuse into the neuron down their gradient.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the neurotransmitter travels through the channel picks this. In fact acetylcholine stays bound on the outside; it is sodium ions that pass through the open pore.
A student who thinks ion movement in neurons is powered by ATP picks this. In fact the receptor is a channel, not a pump: sodium ions diffuse in down their gradient.

A student who has merged the two kinds of gated channel picks this. In fact the nicotinic receptor is opened by acetylcholine binding; it is the voltage-gated channels that respond to the change in potential.

The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a neurotransmitter-gated ion channel. Binding of acetylcholine changes its shape and opens a pore, and sodium ions diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient, depolarizing the membrane.
questions.explain: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a neurotransmitter-gated ion channel. Binding of acetylcholine changes its shape and opens a pore, and sodium ions diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient, depolarizing the membrane.

questions.q: A neuron is treated with a drug that inhibits sodium–potassium pumps. Over the following hours its resting membrane potential declines steadily towards zero. Why does inhibiting the pump have this effect?
options: The drug must also be blocking ion channels, because the pump exchanges one sodium ion for one potassium ion and so cannot affect the potential.
The pump normally exports three sodium ions for every two potassium ions imported, so its net export of positive charge and the ion gradients it maintains are lost.
The pump normally moves sodium ions in and potassium ions out, so without it sodium ions no longer enter and the inside of the cell loses positive charge.
The pump normally opens in response to a change in membrane potential, so without it the voltage-gated channels cannot restore the resting state after an impulse.
optionWhy: A student who takes 'exchange' to mean a one-for-one swap picks this. In fact the exchange is 3:2, so the pump moves net positive charge out of the cell, and the gradients it maintains are what the potential depends on.

Sodium–potassium pumps are important in generating membrane potentials: each cycle moves three positive ions out and two in, and the sodium and potassium gradients this builds are what the resting potential depends on. Without the pump the gradients run down and the potential decays.
A student who has the directions reversed picks this. In fact the pump moves sodium out and potassium in; without it sodium leaks in and potassium leaks out, and the potential collapses.

A student who confuses the pump with a voltage-gated channel picks this. In fact the pump is driven by ATP hydrolysis, not by a change in potential, and it maintains the gradients that the channels rely on.
questions.explain: Sodium–potassium pumps are important in generating membrane potentials: each cycle moves three positive ions out and two in, and the sodium and potassium gradients this builds are what the resting potential depends on. Without the pump the gradients run down and the potential decays.

questions.q: Epithelial cells from the small intestine were treated with a substance that inhibits sodium–potassium pumps. Uptake of glucose from the lumen by the cells fell sharply, although the sodium-dependent glucose cotransporters themselves were not affected by the substance. What explains this result?
options: The inhibitor stopped the cotransporters hydrolysing ATP, which they need to move glucose against its gradient.
Glucose is normally absorbed by simple diffusion, and the inhibitor made the lipid bilayer impermeable to it.
Without the pumps, sodium accumulated in the cells, so there was no sodium gradient to drive glucose uptake.
The pumps normally carry glucose into the cell, so inhibiting them removed the main route for glucose.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the cotransporter uses ATP directly picks this, but the stem says the cotransporters were unaffected. In fact they never hydrolyse ATP; they use the sodium gradient.
A student who thinks glucose diffuses through the bilayer picks this. In fact glucose is polar and cannot cross the bilayer; it needs the cotransporter, and the bilayer was not changed.

The cotransporter moves glucose against its gradient only because sodium ions flow in down theirs. Sodium–potassium pumps maintain that gradient by using ATP to remove sodium from the cell, so inhibiting the pumps removes the gradient and glucose uptake fails. This is why the transport is called indirect active transport.
A student who has not learnt what the pump carries picks this. In fact the pump moves only sodium and potassium ions; glucose enters through the cotransporter, which depends on the pump indirectly.
questions.explain: The cotransporter moves glucose against its gradient only because sodium ions flow in down theirs. Sodium–potassium pumps maintain that gradient by using ATP to remove sodium from the cell, so inhibiting the pumps removes the gradient and glucose uptake fails. This is why the transport is called indirect active transport.

questions.q: Liver cells were broken open in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution and the homogenate was spun in an ultracentrifuge at a series of increasing speeds. Only the pellet formed at the second speed consumed oxygen and produced ATP when supplied with substrates. What does this investigation illustrate about how progress in science is made?
options: Electron micrographs of the organelles in the second pellet would have revealed the same function, so the centrifuge added little that was new.
A technique for isolating one type of organelle made it possible to test its function directly, which could not be done before.
The ATP must have come from intact cells surviving in the pellet, since organelles cannot work once removed from a cell.
A single spin at the highest speed would have brought every organelle down in one pellet that could be tested just as well.
optionWhy: A student who thinks organelle functions were read off from images picks this. A micrograph shows structure only; oxygen consumption and ATP production could only be demonstrated by isolating the organelle and testing it, which needed the ultracentrifuge.

Differential centrifugation separated a fraction rich in mitochondria, and that fraction alone respired. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges and cell fractionation methods had been developed: progress in science often follows a new technique.

A student who extends cell theory to mean that nothing smaller than a cell can carry out a process picks this. Isolated mitochondria in a suitable solution consume oxygen and make ATP; that is exactly what makes cell fractionation informative.

A student who thinks centrifuging merely speeds up settling picks this. A single high-speed spin would bring down every organelle together; only a series of increasing speeds separates nuclei, then mitochondria, then smaller components into different pellets. A mixed pellet could not show which organelle was responsible for the oxygen consumption.
questions.explain: Differential centrifugation separated a fraction rich in mitochondria, and that fraction alone respired. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges and cell fractionation methods had been developed: progress in science often follows a new technique.

questions.q: A gene from a eukaryote is inserted into a bacterium and is transcribed there. In the eukaryotic cell the mRNA from this gene would be modified before translation. What happens to the mRNA in the bacterium?
options: It is modified in the cytoplasm before ribosomes can bind it.
It is translated inside the nucleoid before it is released.
It is not translated, as bacterial ribosomes read the DNA.
It is translated at once, without any modification.
optionWhy: A student who assumes every cell modifies mRNA before translation picks this. A bacterium has no nucleus to hold the mRNA apart from ribosomes, so there is no stage at which modification could happen first.

A student who thinks translation happens where the DNA is, inside a nucleus or its equivalent, picks this. The nucleoid is not a compartment; bacterial ribosomes are in the cytoplasm and bind the mRNA as it is transcribed.
A student who thinks ribosomes can translate DNA directly picks this. Ribosomes in all cells translate mRNA; in a bacterium the mRNA is translated as soon as ribosomes can attach to it.

In prokaryotes there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation, so mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes and be translated, even while it is still being transcribed. Post-transcriptional modification is not possible.
questions.explain: In prokaryotes there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation, so mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes and be translated, even while it is still being transcribed. Post-transcriptional modification is not possible.

questions.q: Electron micrographs of mitochondria from two tissues were analysed. In tissue X the inner membrane had an area of about 40 µm² per µm³ of mitochondrial volume; in tissue Y the value was about 15 µm² per µm³. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: Mitochondria in tissue X absorb oxygen and glucose more quickly through their more extensive cristae.
Mitochondria in tissue X carry out the Krebs cycle faster, since it takes place on the cristae.
Mitochondria in tissue Y store more protons, because a smaller inner membrane leaves a larger intermembrane space.
Mitochondria in tissue X hold more electron transport chains and ATP synthase per unit volume.
optionWhy: A student who links surface area only to absorption picks this. Cristae are folds of the inner membrane and do not increase the area for uptake into the organelle; their area matters for the processes located in the inner membrane.
A student who assigns every mitochondrial process to the cristae picks this. The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix; the inner membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

A student who thinks a bigger proton store is the aim picks this. The data say nothing about the volume of the intermembrane space, and in any case a small space is the adaptation, because it lets a steep gradient form quickly.

The inner membrane, folded into cristae, is where the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are located. More inner membrane area per unit volume means more of these complexes, so a higher capacity for ATP production; this is what the data directly support.
questions.explain: The inner membrane, folded into cristae, is where the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are located. More inner membrane area per unit volume means more of these complexes, so a higher capacity for ATP production; this is what the data directly support.

questions.q: A cell is treated with a substance that blocks all of its nuclear pores. Which consequence would follow?
options: DNA could no longer leave the nucleus to be translated by the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
Protein synthesis would carry on, as ribosomes inside the nucleus would translate the mRNA there.
mRNA could no longer leave the nucleus, so cytoplasmic ribosomes would receive no new mRNA.
mRNA and proteins would still cross the envelope, diffusing through its bilayers as small molecules do.
optionWhy: A student who thinks DNA travels to the ribosomes picks this. DNA never leaves the nucleus; it is mRNA transcribed from the DNA that passes out through the pores.
A student who places translation in the nucleus picks this. There are no functional ribosomes in the nucleus, so mRNA that cannot leave cannot be translated.

The nuclear pores are the only route for mRNA and ribosomal subunits out of the nucleus and for proteins such as polymerases into it. Blocking them cuts off the supply of new mRNA to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm, which is why the double membrane needs pores.

A student who assumes anything can diffuse across a membrane picks this. Large polar molecules such as RNA and proteins cannot cross phospholipid bilayers, which is precisely why the nuclear envelope must have pores.
questions.explain: The nuclear pores are the only route for mRNA and ribosomal subunits out of the nucleus and for proteins such as polymerases into it. Blocking them cuts off the supply of new mRNA to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm, which is why the double membrane needs pores.

questions.q: A vesicle from the Golgi apparatus carries a protein to the plasma membrane for secretion. What happens to the membrane of the vesicle when the protein is released?
options: It passes out through the plasma membrane and is lost from the cell.
It is broken down into phospholipids reused to build the next vesicle.
It stays joined to the Golgi apparatus as a channel for more protein.
It fuses with the plasma membrane and becomes part of it.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the vesicle popping out of the cell picks this. A vesicle cannot pass through a membrane; its bilayer fuses with the plasma membrane and only the contents leave.

A student who thinks vesicle membranes are built and dismantled picks this. Membrane is transferred, not destroyed: the vesicle's bilayer joins the plasma membrane, and new vesicles bud from existing membranes.
A student who imagines continuous channels between organelles picks this. A vesicle is a separate, detached compartment; it buds from the Golgi apparatus and later fuses with the plasma membrane.

In exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the contents outside the cell. The vesicle's phospholipids and proteins are added to the plasma membrane, which is also how the membrane of a growing cell is enlarged.
questions.explain: In exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the contents outside the cell. The vesicle's phospholipids and proteins are added to the plasma membrane, which is also how the membrane of a growing cell is enlarged.

questions.q: In an early-stage embryo a signalling protein is made by cells at one end and spreads towards the other end. Cells at three different distances from the source develop into three different cell types. Which explanation is best supported?
options: The protein is an on/off switch, so the cells that received it differ from the cells that did not.
Different genes are switched on above different concentrations, so each position expresses its own set.
Each cell's fate was fixed internally at fertilization; the protein only marks the region afterwards.
The protein removes different genes from cells at different distances, so each type keeps only the genes it needs.
optionWhy: A student who treats a signal as present or absent picks this. An on/off switch could divide the embryo into two cell types only; three types at three distances show that cells respond to the level of the protein, not merely to its presence.

The protein forms a concentration gradient. Cells respond to the concentration they experience, with different genes switched on at different thresholds, so cells at high, medium and low concentration express different genes and differentiate into three types.

A student who thinks fate is programmed inside each cell from the start picks this. The cells are genetically identical and unspecialized; the gradient is what makes their gene expression differ, so the protein is a cause, not a label.
A student who thinks differentiation removes genes picks this. All the cells keep the whole genome; the gradient changes which genes are expressed at each position, not which genes are present.
questions.explain: The protein forms a concentration gradient. Cells respond to the concentration they experience, with different genes switched on at different thresholds, so cells at high, medium and low concentration express different genes and differentiate into three types.

questions.q: Which pair of properties defines a stem cell?
options: Ability to divide whenever a tissue is damaged and to produce more cells of its own type.
Ability to switch from one specialized type to another whenever a tissue requires this.
Capacity to divide endlessly and ability to differentiate along different pathways.
Continuous division at all times, giving new cells whether or not they are needed.
optionWhy: A student who thinks any cell that divides is a stem cell picks this. Differentiated cells such as fibroblasts divide during repair and produce their own type, but they have limited divisions and cannot differentiate along other pathways.

A student who thinks specialized cells are interchangeable picks this. A stem cell is undifferentiated; it produces other cell types by differentiating, not by converting one specialized type into another.
These are the two defining properties in the guide: a stem cell can divide endlessly, and it can differentiate along different pathways to give specialized cell types. Both are required.

A student who reads 'divide endlessly' as 'divide continuously' picks this. Stem cells have an unlimited capacity to divide but can be maintained in a resting state by their niche; the defining property is the capacity, not constant activity.
questions.explain: These are the two defining properties in the guide: a stem cell can divide endlessly, and it can differentiate along different pathways to give specialized cell types. Both are required.

questions.q: A student argues: 'Real cells are not cubes, so the cube model of surface area-to-volume ratio proves nothing about real cells.' Which response best evaluates this claim?
options: The claim is right: a model is only valid when it has the same shape as the thing that it represents.
The model is simplified on purpose; area and volume scale in the same way for any shape, so its conclusion holds.
The claim is right for another reason: in real cells the surface area and the volume grow in proportion.
The claim is wrong, because in real cells the ratio increases with size, which the simple cube model fails to show.
optionWhy: A student who judges a model by its resemblance to the real thing picks this. The value of a model lies in the relationship it isolates, not in looking like the system; the cube model isolates the effect of size and does so correctly.

Models are simplified versions of complex systems. Cubes are simpler than real cells, but scaling a shape of any kind multiplies area by the square and volume by the cube of the scale factor, so the conclusion that larger cells have a smaller ratio applies to real cells.

A student who scales area and volume in step picks this. In any object, cube or cell, area grows with the square of length and volume with the cube, so they do not grow in proportion; the cube model shows exactly this.

A student who believes the ratio rises with size picks this. In real cells, as in cubes, the ratio falls as size increases; the cube model shows this correctly, which is why the claim is wrong for a different reason.
questions.explain: Models are simplified versions of complex systems. Cubes are simpler than real cells, but scaling a shape of any kind multiplies area by the square and volume by the cube of the scale factor, so the conclusion that larger cells have a smaller ratio applies to real cells.

questions.q: A striated muscle fibre has one continuous plasma membrane and cytoplasm and contains hundreds of nuclei. Which is the best assessment of whether it is a cell?
options: It is not a cell, because a cell by definition contains exactly one nucleus, whereas this muscle fibre contains many hundreds.
It is debatable: one membrane and cytoplasm argue for a cell, but many nuclei and an origin by fusion argue for a syncytium.
It is a cell, because its nuclei arose by repeated mitosis inside a single cell that did not undergo cytokinesis.
It is a cell, because cardiac muscle cells also contain many nuclei, and they are accepted as cells by biologists.
optionWhy: A student who has made 'one nucleus' part of the definition of a cell picks this. Cell theory does not fix the number of nuclei; the nucleus count is one consideration in the debate, not a rule that settles it.

The guide asks for a discussion, not a verdict. A single membrane enclosing a single cytoplasm that works as a unit fits the idea of a cell; hundreds of nuclei and formation from many separate cells fit the idea of a multinucleate structure. Both positions can be defended.

A student who explains the many nuclei by mitosis without cytokinesis picks this. The fibre actually forms by fusion of many myoblasts, and that origin is the main argument against calling it a single cell.

A student who generalizes from skeletal to cardiac muscle picks this. Cardiac muscle cells are short, branched and usually have a single nucleus, so they offer no precedent for accepting a multinucleate fibre as a cell.
questions.explain: The guide asks for a discussion, not a verdict. A single membrane enclosing a single cytoplasm that works as a unit fits the idea of a cell; hundreds of nuclei and formation from many separate cells fit the idea of a multinucleate structure. Both positions can be defended.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches an adaptation of a human gamete to its function?
options: Sperm acrosome: stores the fuel that the mitochondria respire while the sperm swims.
Egg zona pellucida: a cell wall that gives the egg mechanical protection from damage.
Egg and sperm of matching size: each gamete carries half of the chromosomes needed.
Egg cytoplasm with nutrient stores: supplies the embryo's first divisions.
optionWhy: A student who assumes the sperm carries a food store in its head picks this. The acrosome contains enzymes for digesting through the layers around the egg; the midpiece mitochondria respire substrates absorbed from the surrounding fluid.

A student who calls any layer outside the membrane a cell wall picks this. Animal cells have no cell wall; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer that sperm bind to and digest through, then modified to block further sperm.

A student who links equal genetic contribution to equal size picks this. The gametes are extremely different in size: the egg is about 100 µm across and full of cytoplasm, while the sperm is tiny and streamlined for swimming.

The egg is large because its cytoplasm contains stored nutrients (yolk droplets) that supply the embryo during its first divisions, before it can obtain nutrients from the mother. This is why the egg is one of the largest human cells.
questions.explain: The egg is large because its cytoplasm contains stored nutrients (yolk droplets) that supply the embryo during its first divisions, before it can obtain nutrients from the mother. This is why the egg is one of the largest human cells.
